headline: Open Sauce 2026 features $1,700 full-color UV printers and a rideable speeder bike
summary: The quirky maker festival showcased cutting-edge 3D printing, including new desktop UV printers starting at $1,700, offering full-color prints and flash-cured resin. Attendees also saw innovative custom builds like a rideable Star Wars speeder bike.
details: Open Sauce 2026, the quirky maker festival, recently showcased the bleeding edge of 3D printing and custom builds. Highlights included desktop UV printers, which are making industrial technology accessible, and a variety of wild, functional creations.

UV printing, an industrial technology, is now arriving on home desktops with machines starting around $1,700. This process uses UV-cured ink to print photographic color on nearly any material, from flat stickers to "2.5D textures" a few millimeters high, and even venturing into full-color 3D printing.

Several companies, including xTool, EufyMake, and Morpho, are working to shrink these typically $50,000+ industrial machines into more affordable desktop units. xTool, a major sponsor, demonstrated its creator tools and lasers with hands-on stations at the event.

Among the most eye-catching custom builds was a fan-made, rideable Star Wars speeder bike from Snapmaker. This impressive creation was mostly 3D-printed, cleverly concealing an electric scooter underneath to give the illusion of floating.

Other innovations included Unlayered 3D's non-planar 5-axis 3D printer, which defies traditional layered printing with a tilting print head and rotating bed to eliminate supports. Positron 3D also displayed its LDO Positron, an upside-down 3D printer designed to fold down to a compact 200 × 200 × 70 mm.

Prusa Research's booth was a hub of activity, featuring their new CORE One+ INDX alongside other machines. They also presented creative projects like a giant cardboard Core One+ photo booth and an axe-wielding CORE One bot that printed while moving around the venue.

headline_marked: [[Fake 'air conditioner' sold for €163]] contains only a PC fan and heating element
headline: Fake 'air conditioner' sold for €163 contains only a PC fan and heating element
summary: Germany's Stiftung Warentest warns against Epicooler, a device aggressively marketed as an AC unit but which failed to cool rooms in tests. It's essentially a fan and heater.
details: Germany's leading consumer organization, Stiftung Warentest, has exposed the Epicooler as a fraudulent air conditioner. Marketed as an AC unit, it was found to contain only a simple PC fan and a small heating element. Tests showed it failed to reduce room temperature in 'Cold Wind' mode.

The Epicooler is aggressively marketed with AI-generated videos on social media and looks similar to traditional AC units, but sells for a fraction of the price, around €163 ($188). This low price attracts buyers seeking a bargain during Europe's hot summer.

However, consumers are reportedly overpaying for what is essentially an expensive fan. The devices are always shipped from China, even when local stock is advertised, a method believed to help Epicooler evade national regulators and consumer protection laws.
Previous complaints about Epicooler products have surfaced on review sites and social media. Stiftung Warentest's full exposure provides official confirmation of the deceptive practices.

The device's light weight (under 3 kg vs. 13 kg for a genuine internal unit) raised immediate suspicion. A sticker on the unit itself revealed its true nature, reading 'Wall Mounted Heater,' confirming the absence of any genuine cooling components like a compressor.

While cheap for an AC, it's expensive for a fan. Stiftung Warentest noted that accurately advertised fans with better reviews are available for half the Epicooler's price, urging consumers to be cautious.
